z-m-19-01.title: Is √a+√b equal to √(a+b)?
z-m-19-01.topic: How fit you write sum of two square-root numbers?
z-m-19-01.goal: Use one counterexample to show √a+√b=a+b under root no always hold; find pairs (a,b) where sum simplify to one radical, and describe common feature.
z-m-19-01.material: Minjae say, “To add two square roots, add numbers under roots and write one root. Example √2+√3=√5.” Let a,b positive; claim na √a+√b=√(a+b). Reference: √2≈1.414, √3≈1.732, √5≈2.236.

z-m-19-01.s.s1.prompt: To test Minjae claim, use a=9,b=16. √9=3 and √16=4, so sum 7; √(9+16)=√25=5. How best interpret result? [9 16 9 3 16 4 9 16 7 9 16 25 5]

z-m-19-01.s.s1.r.b: To prove claim correct, no number of examples enough; to prove wrong, one counterexample enough. You treat two cases same way.
z-m-19-01.s.s1.o.c: 7 and 5 different, so claim no hold for every positive a,b.
z-m-19-01.s.s1.o.d: 9 and 16 perfect squares, so special; this test no count as evidence.
z-m-19-01.s.s1.r.d: Claim say positive a,b, so perfect squares included. Rejecting test because values look special avoid counterexample.
z-m-19-01.s.s1.explain: If claim say “always,” one failing example (√9+√16=7, √25=5) enough break am. But that only mean claim no always correct; some sums fit still become one radical. Next step look for those.

z-m-19-03.goal: When dem give new x range, keep or change your judgment about the minimum of a quadratic function, and make one range yourself wey vertex no dey inside the range and find the minimum.
z-m-19-03.material: Doha rewrite the quadratic function y=x²−4x+1 as y=(x−2)²−3 and talk say, "The minimum is −3." But depending on the question, the x value range fit change too. For each step, one range (like x is 3 or more and 6 or less) and table of y values from some x values show again. Think about all real x values inside the range.

z-m-19-04.title: Inscribed angles for arcs with same length equal?
z-m-19-04.topic: Inscribed angles and arc length: inscribed angles on arcs of the same length
z-m-19-04.goal: Find the wrong line for this explanation 'if arc lengths are equal, the inscribed angles are equal,' find inscribed angles from equal arcs in circles with different radii, then state the condition wey make claim true.
z-m-19-04.material: Circle O radius na 6 cm, and circle O' (O prime) radius na 12 cm. Arc AB for circle O and arc CD for circle O' both get length 4π cm, and each arc smaller than half circle. Doyun talk say, "Inscribed angles on arcs of the same length are equal," and explain am below. (The inscribed angle ∠APB is the angle at which a point P on the circle, on the side other than arc AB, looks at A and B, and ∠CQD is the same way. ∠APB is read 'angle APB'.)
z-m-19-04.thinking.1: Making number examples to see counterexample structure
z-m-19-04.prereq.0: Inscribed angle on arc half the central angle for that arc (grade 9 level)
z-m-19-04.prereq.1: Arc length 2πr×(x/360) for a central angle x° in a circle of radius r (grade 7 level)
z-m-19-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line for Doyun explanation wey no reliable. (Better choose first wrong line, but you may also choose a line where a wrong conclusion is written because of it.)
z-m-19-04.s.s1.hint.0: Check whether each line follow from the line before, and notice whether both circle radii same or different.
z-m-19-04.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate central angle degrees for 4π arc in each circle separately and compare.
z-m-19-04.s.s1.line.0: Circle O radius 6, circle O' radius 12, and arcs AB and CD both length 4π.
z-m-19-04.s.s1.line.1: Arc lengths equal, so both central angles also equal.
z-m-19-04.s.s1.line.2: Inscribed angle half the central angle, so ∠APB and ∠CQD equal too.
z-m-19-04.s.s1.line.3: So inscribed angles for equal-length arcs always equal.
z-m-19-04.s.s1.explain: First wrong line na line 2. Radius and central angle together determine arc length, so for circles with different radii, equal arc lengths still give different central angles. For circle O, 4π=2π×6×(x/360) give central angle 120°, and for circle O', 4π=2π×12×(x/360) give central angle 60°. So inscribed angles different, 60° and 30°. 'Inscribed angle half the central angle' in line 3 na correct statement, but e depend on wrong line 2, so conclusion wrong, and line 4 too. Line 1 na given condition, so e correct.

z-m-19-04.s.s2.explain: Central angle na 2θ, so the arc length is 2πr×(2θ/360)=πrθ/90. If e be 4π, then rθ=360. If r=6, θ=60; if r=12, θ=30; if r=9, θ=40; if r=4, θ=90. Even with same arc length, bigger radius mean smaller inscribed angle.
